objectives: Survey web map tile architecture (XYZ slippy maps, raster vs. vector tiles, PMTiles).
Compare Leaflet, OpenLayers, Mapbox GL JS, MapLibre, deck.gl, Cesium.
Apply Mapbox Style Spec, OSM tags, Natural Earth, basemap sources.

slides.title: From Google Maps 2005 to PMTiles — tile architecture
slides.body:
**The slippy map revolution (2005-2010)**:
- Before 2005, web maps were either thin GIS-server applets (ArcIMS, GeoServer WMS) or static images. Slow, ugly, brittle.
- **Google Maps (February 8, 2005)** launched with three radical ideas: (1) **continuous panning** via mouse drag rather than clickable nav arrows; (2) **AJAX tile loading** — fetch pre-rendered 256×256 PNG tiles on demand; (3) **fixed zoom levels** with consistent tiling pyramid. Lars + Jens Rasmussen + their team at Where 2 Technologies prototyped + were acquired by Google. Google Maps' UI invented the modern web map.
- **OpenStreetMap (Steve Coast, 2004)** + the OSM tile server adopted the same XYZ tile scheme + made it open. Together, slippy map architecture became the dominant idiom.
- **OpenLayers (MetaCarta, 2006)** + later **Leaflet (Volodymyr Agafonkin, 2011)** open-sourced the client-side library; both still widely used.

**XYZ tile pyramid**:
- **Tiles** are square images (typically 256×256 px) keyed by **(z, x, y)**: $z$ is zoom level (0 = world in 1 tile, 1 = 2×2, ..., $z$ = $2^z \times 2^z$); $x$, $y$ are tile column + row.
- URL convention: `https://server/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` (TMS reverses Y origin; the XYZ + TMS convention difference is a perennial source of bugs).
- **Web Mercator EPSG:3857** is the universal tile projection — projects the world into a square at $z = 0$, doubled tile count at each zoom level.
- Zoom levels 0-22+ in practice; resolution ≈ 156543 / $2^z$ m/pixel at the equator. Z=15 ≈ 5 m/pixel — neighborhood scale.
- **TileJSON** (TileMill + MapBox, 2011) — JSON metadata describing a tileset (URL template, bounds, zoom range, attribution).

**Raster vs. vector tiles**:
- **Raster tiles** — pre-rendered PNG/JPEG/WebP. Easy to serve; fixed style at render time; quick to display; large storage for global high-zoom (terabytes).
- **Vector tiles** — geometric data (points, lines, polygons) sent as **Mapbox Vector Tile (MVT) PBF (Protocol Buffer)** binary. **Style is applied client-side** — the same tile can render in night-mode, dark-mode, hiking-mode, with one tileset. Much smaller storage; supports interactive features (hover, click, label collision); smooth zoom-in via WebGL.
- **MVT (Mapbox 2014)** is now an **OGC standard (2020)**. Encodes features as triangulated geometry + properties + zoom-level-of-significance.
- **Vector tile sources** — OpenMapTiles, Mapbox Streets, Esri Vector Basemaps, MapTiler Cloud.

**PMTiles (Brandon Liu, 2022+)**:
- **PMTiles (Protomaps Tiles)** — a single-file format storing the entire tile pyramid in one binary blob, readable via HTTP range requests directly from object storage (S3, R2, GCS) — **no tile server needed**.
- **Brandon Liu's Protomaps** project + free Daylight-OSM-based world tileset (~110 GB for global vector tiles) democratized self-hosted maps. Combined with **MapLibre GL JS** + a static S3 bucket, you can serve a global vector base map with zero servers.
- Companion: **MBTiles** (Mapbox 2011) — SQLite-based tile container, common for offline + on-prem; **COG** for raster tiles.

**Tile serving stack**:
- **TileServer GL** + **Tegola** + **Mapnik** + **MapServer** + **GeoServer** for self-hosting.
- **OSRM tile + heatmap tiles** generated from PostGIS via **martin** (Rust tile server).
- **t-rex, Tippecanoe (Eric Fischer at Mapbox)** for converting GeoJSON → MVT tiles.

slides.title: Client libraries — Leaflet, OpenLayers, Mapbox GL, MapLibre, deck.gl, Cesium
slides.body:
**Web map clients**:

**Leaflet (Volodymyr Agafonkin, 2011+)**:
- **Volodymyr Agafonkin** (Ukrainian engineer, then at MapBox) released Leaflet in 2011. Lightweight (~40 KB), simple API, raster-tile-focused, mobile-friendly. Powers BBC, NASA, GitHub maps, OSM main site, thousands of projects.
- Best for: static or moderate-traffic raster maps; simple markers + popups; legacy + simple use.
- Extensions: Leaflet.draw, Leaflet.markercluster, Leaflet.heat, Leaflet.VectorGrid (vector tiles).

**OpenLayers (MetaCarta 2006 → OSGeo)**:
- Older + more feature-rich than Leaflet. Supports many projections (not just Web Mercator), WMS, WMTS, GeoTIFF, vector + raster, complex styling.
- Best for: enterprise GIS web apps where you need projection flexibility + advanced features (editing, vector drawing, multiple data sources).

**Mapbox GL JS (Mapbox 2014+)**:
- WebGL-based vector tile renderer. Smooth pan/zoom, dynamic styling, label collision, 3D extrusions, hillshade. Closed-source since Mapbox v2.0 (2020) license change.
- The reference implementation for vector-tile rendering. Mapbox Style Spec is the open style language.

**MapLibre GL JS (community fork, 2020+)**:
- Open-source fork of Mapbox GL JS v1 after the license change. BSD-licensed; community-driven (AWS, Microsoft, Stadia Maps, MapTiler, Felt, etc.).
- API-compatible with Mapbox GL up to v1.13. The default modern open-source choice for vector tile web maps.
- Native versions: MapLibre Native (iOS, Android).

**deck.gl (Uber, 2016+)**:
- WebGL data-viz library for **large-scale geospatial layers** — millions of points, animated flows, hex-bins, GPU-accelerated rendering. Built by Uber Visualization (Nicolas Belmonte + colleagues).
- Composes with Mapbox / MapLibre as a layer; standalone for visualization-heavy use cases. Used by Uber's data products, Felt, Kepler.gl (also from Uber).
- Best for: data-heavy visualization, real-time, animated; not for traditional cartographic styling.

**Cesium + CesiumJS (AGI / Cesium GS, 2011+)**:
- 3D virtual globe in WebGL; supports terrain, 3D Tiles (OGC standard for 3D city models), CZML time-dynamic data, satellite-track visualization.
- Spinoff from Analytical Graphics Inc.; used in defense, simulation, urban digital twins. Open source (Apache).
- 3D Tiles successor: **3D Tiles Next** + **3D Gaussian Splat streaming** for photorealism.

**Other notable**:
- **MapTiler SDK** — commercial wrapper around MapLibre.
- **Carto + CartoDB** — cloud BI maps + visualization.
- **Felt** — collaborative map design (consumer + B2B).
- **Esri ArcGIS JS API** — full Esri ecosystem in browser.
- **Folium (Python)** — Jupyter-friendly wrapper around Leaflet; rapid prototyping.
- **kepler.gl** + **deck.gl** for data-heavy maps; **Observable Plot** + **d3-geo** for custom cartography.

**Mapbox Style Spec**:
- JSON DSL describing map styles — sources, layers, paint, layout, filters, expressions.
- Adopted by MapLibre, Stadia Maps, MapTiler, Tilezen — the de facto standard.
- Style libraries: **Positron, Voyager, Dark Matter (CARTO Basemaps)**, **OSM Bright (OSM standard)**, **Toner, Watercolor (Stamen / Stadia)**, **Esri Vector Basemaps**.
- **Streets, Outdoors, Satellite, Dark, Light** for Mapbox/MapTiler — standard set.

slides.title: Data sources, performance, + the modern web-map stack
slides.body:
**Basemap sources**:

**OpenStreetMap (OSM, 2004+, Steve Coast)**:
- World's largest crowdsourced map database; >10M contributors, billions of nodes + ways.
- **OSM tags** — key-value attributes on nodes/ways/relations. Schema is community-developed at the **OSM Wiki** + **Map Features** page. Highway classification, amenities, natural features.
- Data access: **Overpass API** (read-only query), **Geofabrik regional extracts** (.osm.pbf), **Planet OSM** (~80 GB compressed), **OSMnx (Geoff Boeing)** Python street networks.
- Tile sources: **OSM standard tile server** (rate-limited), **OpenMapTiles** (open vector), **Stadia Maps** (commercial OSM-derived tiles), **Mapbox** (OSM-derived + proprietary).

**Natural Earth (Tom Patterson + Nathaniel Vaughn Kelso, 2009+)**:
- Public-domain reference vector + raster data at 1:10M, 1:50M, 1:110M scales. Country borders, cities, rivers, lakes, ocean, land cover, shaded relief.
- The standard reference data for small-scale base maps; used by NYT, Wikipedia, countless atlases.

**Tilezen / Mapzen + Stamen / Stadia Maps**:
- **Mapzen** (open mapping company, 2013-18) released Tilezen vector tile schema + Pelias geocoder + Valhalla routing; shuttered 2018 but tools live on under **Linux Foundation** governance.
- **Stamen Design** (now Stamen + Stadia Maps) — beautiful artistic basemaps (Toner, Watercolor, Terrain) plus modern Stadia OSM-based tiles. Watercolor was the iconic Stamen style.

**CARTO basemaps**:
- **CartoDB / CARTO Basemaps** — Positron + Dark Matter + Voyager. Minimal, modern, popular for data dashboards. CARTO is also a cloud-native spatial BI platform.

**Esri World Imagery + Living Atlas**:
- Esri's commercial high-resolution global satellite imagery (Maxar, Vivid, USDA NAIP); free in personal use; pay-as-you-go for commercial.
- **Esri Living Atlas** — thousands of curated layers (demographics, environment, hazards).

**Performance + scale techniques**:
- **Tile pyramid + zoom levels** — feature simplification at low zoom; full detail at high zoom. **Tippecanoe (Eric Fischer)** simplifies + decimates for MVT generation.
- **Clustering** — replace overlapping points with summarized markers at low zoom (Leaflet.markercluster, Mapbox cluster, supercluster — also by **Volodymyr Agafonkin**).
- **Heatmaps** — 2D KDE rendered as raster overlay; Mapbox heatmap layer, deck.gl HeatmapLayer.
- **Hex-binning** — H3 (Uber, Sahr 2015) hex grid; deck.gl HexagonLayer; aggregates point data at controllable resolution.
- **WebGL** — GPU rendering of large datasets; **deck.gl, Mapbox GL, MapLibre, CesiumJS, kepler.gl** all use WebGL.
- **Web Workers + streaming** — offload tile parsing + style application to worker threads.
- **HTTP/2 + HTTP/3 + CDN** — parallel tile loading; Cloudflare, Fastly common CDNs.
- **PMTiles + cloud-native** — single-file pyramids on S3 + range requests, no server.
- **Service Workers** — offline + caching for PWAs.

**Modern web-map architecture**:
1. **Data sources** — PostGIS + GeoParquet + Zarr.
2. **Tile generation** — Tippecanoe → MVT → MBTiles or PMTiles.
3. **Tile storage + serving** — S3 / CloudFront (PMTiles), or martin / Tegola tile servers reading PostGIS live.
4. **Style** — Mapbox Style JSON; Maputnik or Visual Studio Code editing.
5. **Client** — MapLibre GL JS (vector) or Leaflet (raster); deck.gl overlay for big data.
6. **Interactivity** — Mapbox GL feature state + queries; deck.gl picking; MapLibre clustering.
7. **Analytics + telemetry** — heatmaps + cluster + spatial joins computed on client or via vector tile properties.

The stack is rich + flexible — from a 200-line Leaflet demo to a Cesium 3D globe to a planet-scale Mapbox commercial deployment, the web-cartography ecosystem has the building blocks for every level of ambition.

question.question: How many tiles at zoom 15 cover the contiguous U.S.?
question.goal: The contiguous U.S. roughly spans longitude -125° to -67° + latitude 25° to 49°. At zoom 15 (Web Mercator), estimate how many tiles cover it.

steps.prompt: How many tiles exist worldwide at zoom $z$? At z = 15?
steps.reveal: $N_{tiles}(z) = 2^z \times 2^z = 4^z$. At $z = 15$: $4^{15} = 2^{30} \approx 1.07 \times 10^9$ — about **a billion tiles** worldwide at zoom 15.

steps.prompt: What fraction of Earth's surface (Web Mercator-projected) is contiguous U.S.?

acceptedAnswers: ~1-2% of Earth surface; ~2-3% in Web Mercator (latitude-distorted at ~35° N)

hints: Continental US ~8 M km²; Earth surface ~510 M km².
steps.reveal: True area: CONUS ~8 M km² out of 510 M km² Earth → ~1.6%. In Web Mercator coordinates the high latitudes inflate, so the **apparent fraction in the projection** ~2-3% at zoom 15. Estimate ~2.5%.

steps.prompt: Approximate tile count for CONUS at zoom 15.
steps.reveal: $\sim 1.07 \times 10^9 \times 0.025 \approx 27$ million tiles for CONUS at $z = 15$. **About 25-30 million tiles** — at 50 KB each, ~1.3 TB of raster tiles for one base style at one zoom level. Vector tiles compress better (~10-20× smaller for typical OSM-style data) — **~50-100 GB** of MVT for the same coverage.

steps.prompt: Why is this why PMTiles + vector tiles matter?

acceptedAnswers: Storage + bandwidth + servers; PMTiles + vector tiles cut cost; styling client-side allows infinite restyling

hints: What does serving a billion tiles cost?
steps.reveal: **Scale economics**: serving a billion raster tiles globally requires a CDN + tile cache + render farm — expensive. **Vector tiles** are ~10-20× smaller + allow client-side restyling (dark mode, hiking mode, language). **PMTiles (Brandon Liu, Protomaps)** stores the whole pyramid in one file on S3, served via HTTP range requests — **no tile server, no rendering, no DB** — democratizes self-hosted global maps. Combined with MapLibre GL JS + a static bucket + a free Daylight-OSM PMTiles file (~110 GB), you can serve a global vector basemap for the price of S3 storage + CloudFront egress. This is the modern open web-map stack.

question.question: Why have **vector tiles + PMTiles** transformed web cartography?
options: **Vector tiles** (Mapbox Vector Tile / MVT, 2014; OGC standard 2020) encode features as geometry + properties in Protocol Buffer binary, **rendered client-side via WebGL**. Advantages over raster tiles: (1) **~10-20× smaller** storage; (2) **client-side styling** — same tileset renders in dark mode, light mode, hiking, satellite-with-labels, with infinite restyling at no server cost; (3) **smooth zoom + label collision** + 3D extrusions via WebGL; (4) **interactivity** — features support hover, click, queryRenderedFeatures; (5) **language switching** via property filters at runtime. **PMTiles (Brandon Liu, Protomaps 2022)** pushes the architecture further: the **entire tile pyramid as a single file** on object storage (S3, R2, GCS), served via HTTP range requests — **no tile server, no database, no rendering** at runtime. Combined with **MapLibre GL JS** (open Mapbox GL fork, 2020) + a Daylight-OSM PMTiles file (~110 GB global vector tiles), a static S3 bucket + CloudFront CDN serve a planet-scale base map for storage cost only. The combination democratizes self-hosted maps: indie developers + NGOs + academics can run global mapping infrastructure that previously required tile servers + render farms + commercial APIs. With vector tiles + PMTiles + MapLibre, the modern web cartography stack is open, cheap, + extensible.
question.explanation: Vector tiles (MVT 2014, OGC 2020) are ~10-20× smaller than raster, support client-side styling (dark/light/hiking from one tileset), smooth WebGL zoom, interactivity, language switching. PMTiles (Brandon Liu / Protomaps 2022) packs entire pyramid in a single file on object storage served via HTTP range requests — no tile server. With MapLibre GL JS (open Mapbox GL fork) + Daylight-OSM PMTiles + static S3, planet-scale base maps cost only storage.

hints: What changed about how styles get applied?
slides.workedSolution: Vector tiles (MVT/MapBox 2014, OGC 2020) + client-side rendering: smaller, restylable, smooth, interactive, multilingual. PMTiles (Brandon Liu / Protomaps 2022) packages whole pyramid as single S3 file with HTTP range reads — no tile server. Plus MapLibre GL JS, modern web maps are open, cheap, planet-scale.

question.question: Architect a public-interest open web mapping platform
question.prompt: Your civic-tech NGO needs to deploy a free public web map for their region (a metropolitan area, ~5 million people, ~10000 km²) showing real-time air quality, weather, transit, environmental hazards. Budget: minimal. Goal: long-term self-sustainable. Design the architecture. Address: (1) **Basemap choice** — OSM via OpenMapTiles vs. self-hosted PMTiles from Daylight-OSM extract vs. Stadia Maps subscription; tradeoffs; (2) **Tile storage** — static S3 + CloudFront vs. martin tile server reading PostGIS; (3) **Vector vs. raster** — why vector tiles for the basemap + raster tiles for the air-quality overlay (gridded sensor data); (4) **Client library** — **MapLibre GL JS (Volodymyr Agafonkin lineage via fork)** for vector basemap, **deck.gl** for animated transit + flows, optional **Leaflet** fallback for low-power devices; (5) **Style** — Mapbox Style Spec JSON; design Positron-style minimal basemap to let overlays pop; multilingual labels via filter expressions; (6) **Real-time data** — air quality from PurpleAir + AirNow; transit GTFS-Realtime; render via vector tile or GeoJSON via WebSocket; (7) **Performance** — clustering (supercluster), H3 hex-bin (deck.gl HexagonLayer) for aggregations, web workers for heavy parse, CDN cache; (8) **3D + perspective** — terrain via Mapbox Terrain-RGB / MapLibre terrain support, optional Cesium for 3D buildings; (9) **Source attribution** — OSM contributors, Natural Earth, project data; (10) **Sustainability** — minimal infra (static S3 + Cloudflare), no proprietary APIs, open code; Brandon Liu's Protomaps blog posts as a model. Deliver an architecture diagram + a tech-stack summary + a cost estimate.

question.question: At Web Mercator zoom level 12, what is the approximate ground resolution per pixel at the equator (in meters, to nearest meter)?
question.hint: Resolution = $156543.03 / 2^z$ m/pixel at the equator. At $z = 12$: $156543 / 4096 \approx 38$ m/pixel. (At z=15: ~5 m; at z=18: ~0.6 m.) This is the base scale before cos(latitude) Web Mercator scaling.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain (1) the slippy-map tile architecture; (2) raster vs. vector tiles + PMTiles; (3) the modern client + style + data ecosystem.
question.rubric: Mentions: **Slippy maps** invented by **Google Maps 2005** (Lars + Jens Rasmussen): continuous panning + AJAX tile fetch + zoom pyramid. **XYZ tile scheme**: 256×256 tiles keyed by (z, x, y) in Web Mercator EPSG:3857; $4^z$ tiles at level z. **TileJSON** metadata. **Raster tiles** (PNG/JPEG, fixed style) vs. **vector tiles** (MapBox MVT 2014, OGC 2020 — PBF binary, client-side styling, ~10-20× smaller, WebGL rendering, interactive, restylable). **PMTiles (Brandon Liu, Protomaps 2022)** — single-file pyramid on object storage, no tile server. **Clients**: **Leaflet (Volodymyr Agafonkin 2011)** lightweight raster, **OpenLayers** enterprise, **Mapbox GL JS (2014, closed since v2)** + **MapLibre GL JS (open fork 2020)** vector WebGL, **deck.gl (Uber 2016)** big-data WebGL, **Cesium** 3D globe, **Folium** Python prototyping. **Mapbox Style Spec** is the de facto style DSL. **Sources**: **OSM (Steve Coast 2004)** + **Natural Earth (Patterson + Kelso)** + **Stamen / Stadia + CARTO + Esri World Imagery**. **Performance**: vector tiles, clustering (supercluster — Agafonkin), heatmap, H3 hex (Uber), WebGL, CDN. **Modern open stack**: PMTiles on S3 + MapLibre GL JS + Mapbox Style + OSM data = planet-scale free maps.
